newsitem.title: UK: UK-S.Africa air cargo trade dives - Reuters survey.
newsitem.headline: UK-S.Africa air cargo trade dives - Reuters survey.

text.p: Air cargo business from the UK to South Africa has suffered badly during the first half of this year due to strong sterling against the rand and increased competition amongst carriers, a Reuters survey showed.
And many participants in the trade foresee little chance of an upturn in their fortunes until at least the pre-Christmas peak season.
Virgin Atlantic Cargo noted airfreight business southbound on the route had been "devastated" since January.

"In that time, some of our shipper and freight forwarder customers have reported 50 percent declines in their South African business as the weak rand against sterling has made it extremely expensive for South African companies to import from Britain," said David Woodward, Virgin's general manager commercial.
"As volumes have dropped and capacity has increased, cargo rates have been put under pressure," he said.

Virgin flies six weekly Airbus A340 London Heathrow-Johannesburg services, which can uplift 15-17 tonnes of cargo, and the frequency will rise to daily from July 15, primarily to cater for additional summer passenger traffic.
Sharon Wright, of airfreight wholesaler Air Menzies International (AMI), forecast that for the UK to Johannesburg air cargo market, "worse is to come".
She also pointed to the weak rand depressing demand, coupled with extra capacity continuing to come on line.

South African Airways said that although southbound ex-London rates had been falling since the start of 1997, cargo capacity was now on the rise as extra flights - catering for vacation and VFR (visiting friends and relatives) traffic - were operated.
"Everyone predicts a slow summer for airfreight as factories close down for the holidays," said SAA UK cargo spokesman Ben Audibert.
"We are flying about 90 percent full (of cargo), but rates have dropped. The strong pound versus the rand has meant South Africans just can't import as much as in the past," he said.

SAA operates 15 weekly 747 Heathrow-Johannesburg 747 services, which offer a combined 225 tonnes' cargo capacity. A further 15 tonnes will come on line with a 16th frequency in October," stated Audibert.
Gil Harding, director of Air Gabon's UK cargo agent ANA Aviation Services, said the ex-UK to South Africa air cargo market was now just a shadow of its former self.

"Over the past year, we have seen yields dropping dramatically. We hear of rates being regularly quoted at below one stg a kg for one-tonne plus, when a year ago the level was at least 1.25 stg," he said.
To counter this decline in business, Harding said ANA/Air Gabon had transferred more of its attention towards the UK-West Africa market.
"About 90 percent of our loads were to South Africa, but this has been reduced to 60 percent," he said.

"We are able to switch our attention to West Africa as Air Gabon now operates Boeing 767 aircraft from Libreville to Angola and other points along the coast, giving us a palletised cargo connection from London," he said.

ANA also acts as agent for DAS Air Cargo, which is planning to expand to southern Africa, definitely including Lusaka, Zambia, later this month and in October, said commercial manager Andy King who declined to give further details.
It has the capacity to do this following the airline's retrieval of a DC-10F it had been leasing to financially troubled Zimbabwean state-owned cargo airline Affretair.

DAS Air already serves a number of African destinations from London Gatwick and Amsterdam, including Zambia, Tanzania, Uganda, Kenya, Ghana and Sierra Leone, with one Boeing 707 freighter (a second is undergoing maintenance work) and the DC-10F, plus connecting flights..
A second DC-10F will join the fleet in October when use of the 707Fs will be phased down.

"Although we are primarily involved in carrying fruit and vegetables from Africa to Europe, southbound ex-UK we are generally full with consumer goods, general freight and relief cargo. The market is steady...it is business as per usual for us," said Leslie.
Added Harding: "Southbound from the UK, the market is reasonably healthy to some destinations, but nothing more than that."

Meanwhile, Air Malawi is experiencing a boom time with its weekly Stansted-Lilongwe freighter service, using a DC-8-55F wet-leased from UK-owned, Ghana-registered MK Airlines, said assistant UK cargo manager Sylvia Drake.
"During most of the year, we share the 38-tonnes' capacity 50-50 with MK, which flies onward to Nairobi and Accra," she said.
"But Malawi students are now returning home from the UK for the summer, taking with them all sorts of consumer items. At present, we are filling up the southbound flight," she added.
Air Malawi has also negotiated the operation of a second weekly northbound MK DC-8F charter from Lilongwe to Stansted from September to cater for Malawi's growing flower export market.
Flower growers in the country had been complaining about the lack of space available after KLM's withdrawal from the Malawi-Europe route in April.
MK Airlines owns and flies four DC-8-55s, three of which are freighters and one a combi, said commercial manager Rob Holland.

While the combi is used for entertainment industry charters, the freighters are wet-leased to Air Malawi and the likes of Lufthansa, British Airways and Air Namibia (for Windhoek-Spain produce flights).
"We specialise in flights from Luxembourg and the UK to Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria and Malawi and most space is pre-sold," said Holland.

From Nairobi, he said that MK was flying 180-200 tonnes of fresh fruit and vegetables a week into the UK. Ex-UK flights to Ghana and Nigeria were also operated on behalf of different freight forwarders.

The two-month-long tit-for-tat British-Nigerian ban on each other's aircraft continues with no sign of a breakthrough, but use of charter and transhipment flights has meant little or no interruption in air cargo flow between the two countries, said airline sources.
MK's Holland said UK-Kenya continued to be a low-yield operation, particularly during the winter when competition was especially strong from Continental Europe-based freighter operators.
Elsewhere, Cameroon Airlines is doing "pretty well" cargo-wise with its weekly 35-tonnes cargo capacity 747 Combi Gatwick-Douala service, said UK cargo manager Jim Walsh.
"Our main considerations now are flying oil-related goods for the Chad-Cameroon Atlantic coast pipeline," he added.
"Our freight is outsized and of strange dimensions for this project -- lengths of pipes and so on -- but for that the Combi is ideal," he said.
Walsh noted that 90 percent of his ex-UK cargo lift is bound for Cameroon, with the rest airfreighted onward to Malabo, Equatorial Guinea, where offshore oil exploration work is underway.
He added that talk was now afoot about extending Cameroon Air's London-Douala Combi flights on to Lagos, a route extension he believed offered "lots of cargo traffic potential".

"While Lagos is a busy, competitive airfreight destination, with our Combi we could offer something different. We could find a niche in the market by catering for heavy machinery, generator and project cargo main-deck shipments, which 707Fs can't handle," he said.
Ethiopian Airlines, meanwhile, is experiencing "reasonably good" cargo business on its Europe-Addis Ababa routes, although "it could be better", said UK cargo manager Peter Talkington.
"The strength of the pound does not appear to be affecting us but then, unlike many other carriers, we are usually busy in the summer months and quiet in the winter," he added.
